questions.ask: Write the action plan for bed 3 from its latest scan.

runs.text:
Bed 3's tomatoes have confirmed early blight at the east end; the fruit is still clean. Bed 3 has already had the six copper sprays the farm's SOP allows for this season, so this plan relies on non-chemical steps. Cut off infected leaves and stems. Mulch the soil. Water only through the drip line in the early morning. Pull weeds and volunteer plants. Check the bed every few days. For next year, rotate tomatoes out of Bed 3, test the soil and choose resistant varieties.

Cut off infected leaves and branches

Start at the east end of Bed 3, where the blight is. Cut off leaves and branches showing target-ring spots, including any stems with lesions, and throw them away. Do not compost them. Work when the leaves are dry, and clean your pruners between plants so you don't carry spores along the row. Repeat as new spots appear.

Mulch the soil under the plants

Spread a layer of organic mulch, such as chopped leaves or straw, over the bare soil under the plants. It stops spores splashing up from the soil onto the leaves.

Keep the leaves dry: drip, early morning

Water only through the drip line along the north edge of the bed, in the early morning, so the leaves are dry by midday. Don't water from above. The west end sits low and dries slowly after rain, so let standing water drain away from it.

Check for spread every 3 days

Walk the whole bed and look for new target-ring spots, especially west of the east end, and check the fruit for dark sunken spots. Bed 3 has had all six copper sprays the farm's SOP allows this season, the last on 2026-09-04, so no more copper is planned. If the disease spreads quickly, ask your local extension office for advice.

Pull weeds and volunteer tomatoes

Pull weeds in and around Bed 3, especially black nightshade, which carries early blight. Pull up any tomato or potato plants that come up on their own.

Pick early blight resistant varieties for 2027

For next season, choose tomato varieties that are resistant or tolerant to early blight. Buy certified disease-free seed or plants.

Test the soil and keep potassium up

Test Bed 3's soil before planting. Keep potassium at a good level and lime only if the test says to. Follow the soil test and the fertiliser label for any amounts.

Rotate tomatoes out of Bed 3

The fungus survives in old plant debris in the soil. Don't plant tomatoes, potatoes, peppers or eggplant in Bed 3 for the next two seasons. Grow a crop that doesn't get these diseases instead; corn is a good choice. Wherever the tomatoes go, space them so the plants don't touch.

New target-ring spots west of the east end within a week, even after you remove infected leaves

Dark, sunken spots on the fruit within the next two weeks

Leaves yellowing and dropping faster than you can remove them within a week; if this happens, contact your local extension office

runs.text:
Early blight is confirmed on Bed 3. It is still limited to the east end, and the fruit is clean. Bed 3 has had all the copper sprays the SOP allows this season, so the plan relies on non-chemical steps: cut off spotted leaves, keep the leaves dry with drip watering in the early morning, mulch, pull weeds, and check the bed every few days. At season end, clear the bed, rotate tomatoes and related crops away from it for three years, test the soil, and choose resistant varieties.

Cut off spotted leaves and stems

Cut off the leaves and stems with target-ring spots, starting at the east end where the blight has been since early September. Throw them away; don't compost them or leave them on the bed. Clean the pruners between plants, and do this when the leaves are dry.

Keep the leaves dry: drip only, early morning

Keep watering only with the drip line along the north edge. Water in the early morning so the leaves are dry by midday, and never water from above. The west end sits low and stays wet after rain, so help standing water drain away there.

Mulch the soil under the plants

Cover bare soil under the plants with organic mulch such as straw or chopped leaves. It stops spores splashing up from the soil onto the leaves.

Pull weeds and self-sown tomatoes

Pull weeds in and around Bed 3, especially black nightshade, which carries early blight. Pull up any tomatoes that come up on their own.

Check the bed for new spots every 3 days

Walk the whole bed and look for new target-ring spots, above all west of the east end, and for any spots on stems or fruit. Copper is not an option for the rest of this season: the spray log shows Bed 3 has had the six applications the SOP allows. If spread speeds up, ask your local extension office for advice.

Clear the bed at season end and rotate

When the plants finish, remove all tomato vines, leaves and fallen fruit from the bed and throw them away. Then don't grow tomatoes, potatoes, peppers or eggplant in Bed 3 again until three years have passed; corn or another grass-family crop is a good choice in between.

Test the soil and keep potassium up

Test the Bed 3 soil before next season. Keep potassium at a good level and lime as the soil test advises; this makes early blight less severe. Follow the soil test and the fertiliser label.

Choose early-blight-resistant varieties for next year

For next year's tomatoes, wherever they go, choose varieties that are resistant or tolerant to early blight. Use certified disease-free seed and transplants.

New target-ring spots spreading west of the east end within a week of removing the spotted leaves

Spots or dark sunken patches on fruit at any time

Lower leaves yellowing and dropping faster over the next two weeks despite pruning and drip-only watering

New spots on stems near the soil line within two weeks

runs.text:
Early blight is confirmed on Bed 3's Celebrity tomatoes. The spots are on upper leaves and a few stems at the east end. The latest field report says it hasn't spread beyond the east end and the fruit is still clean. The spray log shows Bed 3 had its sixth copper spray on 4 September, which is the season limit in the farm's SOP, so this plan adds no more fungicide this season. Instead it slows the disease by removing spotted leaves, keeping the leaves dry, mulching, clearing weeds and draining the low west end. It ends with a rotation and variety choices so next year starts clean.

Cut off spotted leaves at the east end

Go along the east end of Bed 3, where the target-ring spots are, and cut off spotted leaves and any badly spotted small branches. Bag them and throw them away. Don't compost them or leave them on the soil. Work when the leaves are dry, and clean your pruners afterwards so you don't carry spores to clean plants. Leave enough healthy leaves to shade the fruit.

Water at the base with the drip line in the early morning

Keep watering only through the drip line along the north edge of the bed. Avoid overhead watering. Run it in the early morning so any wet leaves dry by midday. Don't water late in the day.

Cover bare soil under the plants with mulch

Top up the organic mulch, such as straw or chopped leaves, over any bare soil under the plants. It stops spores splashing up from the soil onto the leaves.

Check the bed for new ring spots

Walk the whole bed, west end included. Look for new dark spots with rings on the leaves, on the stems and on the fruit. Note whether the spots are moving beyond the east end. If they reach the fruit or spread fast, post a clear photo or ask your local extension office for advice.

Pull weeds and self-sown tomatoes

Pull up weeds in and around Bed 3, especially black nightshade, which carries early blight. Pull up any tomato or potato plants that have come up on their own nearby. Bag them and throw them away.

Drain standing water from the low west end after heavy rain

The west end of Bed 3 sits low and is slow to dry. After heavy rain, open a shallow channel or clear the path edge so standing water drains away quickly. Keep the plants growing strongly with steady drip watering.

Plan a three-year rotation for Bed 3

Once frost ends the season, plan next year's beds so that tomatoes, potatoes, peppers and eggplant don't go back into Bed 3 for at least three years. A crop such as corn is a good choice for the bed in between. Remove the old tomato plants and debris from the bed so the disease has less to survive on.

Choose early-blight-tolerant varieties for next year

When ordering seed for next year, choose tomato varieties sold as resistant or tolerant to early blight. Buy certified, disease-free seed or plants.

Ring spots appearing beyond the east end, or in the west end, within the next week

Dark sunken spots on the fruit within the next two weeks

Leaves yellowing and dropping across most of the bed within ten days despite leaf removal

plan.summary: Early blight is confirmed on Bed 3's Celebrity tomatoes. The spots are on upper leaves and a few stems at the east end. The latest field report says it hasn't spread beyond the east end and the fruit is still clean. The spray log shows Bed 3 had its sixth copper spray on 4 September, which is the season limit in the farm's SOP, so this plan adds no more fungicide this season. Instead it slows the disease by removing spotted leaves, keeping the leaves dry, mulching, clearing weeds and draining the low west end. It ends with a rotation and variety choices so next year starts clean.

steps.title: Cut off spotted leaves at the east end
steps.detail: Go along the east end of Bed 3, where the target-ring spots are, and cut off spotted leaves and any badly spotted small branches. Bag them and throw them away. Don't compost them or leave them on the soil. Work when the leaves are dry, and clean your pruners afterwards so you don't carry spores to clean plants. Leave enough healthy leaves to shade the fruit.

steps.title: Water at the base with the drip line in the early morning
steps.detail: Keep watering only through the drip line along the north edge of the bed. Avoid overhead watering. Run it in the early morning so any wet leaves dry by midday. Don't water late in the day.

steps.title: Cover bare soil under the plants with mulch
steps.detail: Top up the organic mulch, such as straw or chopped leaves, over any bare soil under the plants. It stops spores splashing up from the soil onto the leaves.

steps.title: Check the bed for new ring spots
steps.detail: Walk the whole bed, west end included. Look for new dark spots with rings on the leaves, on the stems and on the fruit. Note whether the spots are moving beyond the east end. If they reach the fruit or spread fast, post a clear photo or ask your local extension office for advice.

steps.title: Pull weeds and self-sown tomatoes
steps.detail: Pull up weeds in and around Bed 3, especially black nightshade, which carries early blight. Pull up any tomato or potato plants that have come up on their own nearby. Bag them and throw them away.

steps.title: Drain standing water from the low west end after heavy rain
steps.detail: The west end of Bed 3 sits low and is slow to dry. After heavy rain, open a shallow channel or clear the path edge so standing water drains away quickly. Keep the plants growing strongly with steady drip watering.

steps.title: Plan a three-year rotation for Bed 3
steps.detail: Once frost ends the season, plan next year's beds so that tomatoes, potatoes, peppers and eggplant don't go back into Bed 3 for at least three years. A crop such as corn is a good choice for the bed in between. Remove the old tomato plants and debris from the bed so the disease has less to survive on.

steps.title: Choose early-blight-tolerant varieties for next year
steps.detail: When ordering seed for next year, choose tomato varieties sold as resistant or tolerant to early blight. Buy certified, disease-free seed or plants.

watch_for: Ring spots appearing beyond the east end, or in the west end, within the next week
Dark sunken spots on the fruit within the next two weeks
Leaves yellowing and dropping across most of the bed within ten days despite leaf removal
